Ana, the Meyer contract. It has been sitting there for two months. What is actually going on?
Their counsel drew up the first version in March. We carried out our part — the technical annex went over in April.
And then it just stopped. Why?
One clause held it up. Liability. And while we were still ironing out the wording, the term rolled over, so the old prices stayed.
So we lost two months over a single clause.

Worse. Last week the supplier backed out of the whole thing and the deal fell through. Their competitor has offered to take over the same scope. This time I would spell out the liability cap in the very first draft.
Agreed — we spell it out before anybody signs. Send me the competitor's name and I will move on it today.

I have worked with lawyers from about fifteen countries, and there is one thing I noticed early, and it took me years to understand what I was hearing. Their English was excellent. Technically perfect. And it was strange. Not wrong. Strange. They spoke the way a contract is written. The agreement was executed on the twelfth of March. The supplier subsequently terminated the arrangement. Nobody in an American office talks like that. We say: we drew it up on the twelfth. They backed out in June. And here is the part that surprised me. I always assumed that formal language sounded like authority. It does not. It sounds like distance. When somebody speaks to me in written English, I hear a document, not a person, and I stop asking questions, because it feels like there is nobody there to ask. So my advice is simple, and it is not about being casual. Keep the Latin verbs for the page. On a call, use the two word verbs. Same meaning, different room. You will sound closer, and people will interrupt you, which is exactly what you want.

For about eight months I said two things wrong, every week, in front of the same people. I said back out the deal, and I said draw up it. Nobody corrected me. Not once. They understood me perfectly, so why would they? I only found out because I recorded myself for a different reason and heard it. That was not the useful part, though. The useful part was what I changed afterwards. I had been studying phrasal verbs the way everybody does, from a list, in alphabetical order. Back out, break down, call off, carry out. Fifty of them on a page. I could recognize all fifty and produce none of them, because a list has no situation in it, and my mouth needs a situation. So I stopped. Now I learn them inside one story. The story I use is a deal. Somebody draws it up, we carry it out, we iron out the open points, the term rolls over, someone backs out, the thing falls through. Once a week I tell that whole story out loud, from the first draft to the collapse. Six months of that, and the verbs come when I need them.
